---
title: "Deriving proxy weights for web scraped data"
date-modified: "2021-10-05"
---

Web scraped data does not contain expenditure information. In some
cases, proxy expenditure weights can be derived.\

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Introduction {#Derivingproxyweightsforwebscrapeddata-Introduction}

In contrast to scanner data, web scraped data are not transaction data
which means that they do not contain information on the quantities sold.
Especially in the dynamic universe of online trading, it would be
important to know if a price that has been observed is really relevant
in terms of the number of transactions that have been taken place at
this price. Research has shown this is rarely the case and while
consumers purchase a variety of products, they exhibit strong preference
for only a small subsection of the available products and brands within
any item. Antoniades et al. (2019) on distribution as expenditure found
that typically sales distribution is so skewed, that based on their
calculations total sales of the top 2% of grocery products per item
accounted for as much as the total sales of the bottom 96%. 

The lack of information on the quantities sold entails two issues that
have to be dealt with when web scraped data are used to compute price
indices, aggregation of prices across time and how proxy expenditure
weights can be calculated and used in the calculation of price indices.

# Aggregation of prices over time {#Derivingproxyweightsforwebscrapeddata-Aggregationofpricesovertime}

First, a decision has to be made on how different prices for the same
item are aggregated over time (for example for a month or a quarter).
Usually, the prices observed at different times of the month (or
quarter) are aggregated to an unweighted (equally) weighted average
price, which reflects the assumption that the buying behaviour with
respect to a specific item is more or less independent of the price.
Even though this is likely to be a too strong assumption, past research
projects such as Chessa & Griffioen (2019) did not find severe
differences between unit values based on scanner data and the respective
average prices based on web scraped data. As expected, unit values were
often found to be lower or equal compared to the average web scraped
prices. Different factors may offer an explanation for this observation,
such as different forms of discount that may enter transaction prices
which cannot be scraped (e.g. discounts for customer card holders) and
also increases in the numbers of items sold during discount periods. It
is important to keep in mind that there seem to be only a few examples
of such comparative studies (perhaps due to the difficult in sourcing
different data for the same retailer), and that the cited study applies
to a web-only shop. Further research could be conducted to verify
whether the unweighted average price is appropriate also for products
and/or retailers with both physical outlets and web shops, and for
products/retailers with a very dynamic pricing strategy. In this
context, it is worth mentioning that for the purpose of calculating the
Consumer Price Index (CPI), the prices which are used for the index
calculation must not necessarily reflect the true price level but the
true price development. This means that the bias of the average price
level could be greater than the bias of the change in the average price
level.

# Calculation of proxy weights {#Derivingproxyweightsforwebscrapeddata-Calculationofproxyweights}

Second, the lack of information on quantities sold is an issue when it
comes to price index calculations. ONS (2020) found that unweighted
indices may suffer from a notable bias compared to their weighted
counterparts. In order to mitigate this bias, some research has been
conducted on deriving proxy weights for web scraped data. Two different
approaches have arisen which are introduced in the following paragraphs.

Chessa & Griffioen (2019) used the number of times an item was scraped
as a proxy for the quantities sold for this item. In their study, they
compared web scraped data and scanner data from the same retailer. The
website of the retailer was fully scraped which means that an item could
have been scraped on different \"routes\", i.e. when navigating from the
main menu through the various submenus. For example, an item from the
retailer analysed by Chessa & Griffioen (2019) could be found in the sub
menu \"mens' clothing\" but also in the sub menu \"sales\". Chessa &
Griffioen (2019) observed in their data a remarkable correlation between
the number of prices scraped with this technique and the quantities sold
based on the scanner data of the same retailer. The price indices
calculated with these proxy weights were much closer to the benchmark
prices indices based on scanner data than the unweighted price indices.
Even though the results were promising, the authors recommended to
verify whether these findings apply also to other retailers.

A different approach was conducted by Touzani & van Buskirk (2015) and
ONS (2020). They used the popularity rankings defined by the order (or
rather position) of where products are published on the website of a
retailer. Thereby, they assumed that the cumulative distribution of the
rank order was equal to the cumulative distribution of the number of
sales. Given a log normal distribution, a truncated log normal
distribution and a Pareto distribution, ONS (2020) determined the
required distribution parameters by a maximum likelihood estimation
based on summary statistics which were available in a scanner data set
of the same retailer. In a next step, the sales quantities were derived
from the equation of the cumulative distribution function of the rank
order on the website and the suggested cumulative distribution function
of the quantities sold. These approximated sales quantities were then
used in a final step to calculate price indices. The results indicated
that especially the truncated log, normal distribution could reduce the
bias as measured with respect to the scanner data indices in comparison
to the unweighted index series. It is important to note that this kind
of approach requires the retailers to provide summary statistics, which
means that some kind of cooperation with a retailer is needed and it
relies on the (strong) assumption that the order in which products
appear on retailers' websites is reflective of quantities sold. For some
retailers, it is possible to sort by \"popularity\" which could infer
this relationship. However, for some retailers this option is not
possible and they either don\'t allow sorting, or use the vaguer term
\"relevance\". In some cases, retailers may influence the order to
ensure that those products with larger profit margins sit at the top of
the list rather than those with high quantities sold. This means that
this approach should be used only when it can be reasonably assumed that
the position of the product on the website indeed reflects the order of
quantities sold because otherwise, there is a danger that the bias gets
even worse compared to an unweighted index.

Possible alternatives for deriving proxy weights also include (research
still ongoing): scraping the number of reviews for each product as a
proxy for expenditure, testing the market share approach outlined in
Antoniades et al. (2019), and using the theory of \"price banding\". The
principle around the price band approach is a simplistic one, that
producers know the optimum price they can sell their product to maximise
sales. We can deduce that the more products around a certain price point
will contain the highest selling products of the item, because more
producers recognise the price as the optimum selling price. In practice,
this means that each item is split into multiple price bands and each
product can then be assigned to a band based on its price. The bands are
then ranked from most products to least, with the products in the most
populated price band receiving more weight than the products in the less
populated price bands. As these research projects complete, we will link
to the published results on this page.

# Alternative approaches {#Derivingproxyweightsforwebscrapeddata-Alternativeapproaches}

Apart from these approaches to calculate proxy weights, one could also
think about other ways to reduce the bias of unweighted indices for web
scraped data. One option could be to use a bestseller approach where a
certain number of the most popular items would be selected for the price
collection via web scraping. The required bestseller lists could be
searched on product specific websites or magazines. This approach would
exclude items rarely sold from the price collection, which again might
increase the representativity of the index results. Another approach
that could be investigated is the use of weights from external sources.
Even when these weights might not be available on the item level, they
could help to distinguish more relevant from less relevant product
groups (in terms of expenditure shares) such that an implicit or
explicit weighting could be applied at the level of product groups. For
example, weight information may be available at the brand level for
technology products that could then be used to approximate the weight
for individual items.

This is an area of ongoing research and it is clear that more work is
necessary to shed more light on the issue of deriving proxy weights for
web scraped data.
